title: International confidence in the United States as a partner is weaker than formal alliance ties
source_unit: Pew Research Center survey of adults in 36 countries, conducted in spring 2026
geography: United States viewed from 36 surveyed countries

us_favorable_median.unit: percent median favorable view of the United States

us_unfavorable_median.unit: percent median unfavorable view of the United States

us_considers_interests_median.unit: percent median saying the U.S. considers countries like theirs' interests a great deal or fair amount

observations.method: Pew Research Center cross-national survey of public views of the United States, its reliability as a partner, and whether it considers other countries' interests; country medians and named-country shares are retained separately.
observations.uncertainty: International opinion is not a direct measure of diplomatic behavior, alliance compliance, military access, trade, aid, or deterrence. Country medians are not population-weighted global estimates, and cross-sectional comparisons do not identify the cause of change.
observations.subgroup: Adults in 36 surveyed countries, including NATO member and nonmember states; country results vary substantially.
observations.counterinterpretation: Views may reflect current leadership, a specific conflict, domestic politics, historical memory, or general attitudes toward U.S. power rather than a settled judgment about a particular alliance or policy.

boundary: This record adds an external-reception layer to the geopolitical atlas. It does not establish that lower confidence changed a government decision, alliance operation, public protest, trade relationship, deterrence outcome, or adversary behavior.
